newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Kim names "Mr Clean" to head his party.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Kim names "Mr Clean" to head his party.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam has named a respected former judge, dubbed "Mr Clean", as the new chairman of his ruling party in a surprise move seen as a bid to avert a political crisis.
The nomination of Lee Hoi-chang would be confirmed at a caucus of the New Korea Party later on Thursday, a presidential Blue House official said.

Lee, 61, is best known for quitting as Kim's prime minister in 1994 to protest curbs on his power. By standing up to the president, he strengthened his reputation for independence and for refusing to compromise his principles.

Political analysts said Kim, desperate to avert a crisis stemming from a loans scandal and suspected influence peddling by his son, appeared to have accepted he was becoming a lame duck leader in his final year in office.
A senior government official who is close to the president said Lee would now have a "clear advantage" in a race to win party candidacy for presidential elections in December.
Lee is one of nine party leaders -- known as the "nine dragons" -- tipped as contenders for the party's presidential nomination.
Kim is barred by the constitution from seeking a second five-year term but analysts say he has tried to work behind the scenes to put in place a successor.

"The appointment of Lee as party chairman demonstrates how desperate Kim is. He is cornered by the current crisis," Cho Chang-hyun, political science professor at Seoul's Hanyang University, told Reuters.

"Lee is the most difficult figure for Kim to handle," Cho said. "To some extent, Kim will have to share power with Lee. He is running out of options and he may be using his last card." Lee added to his reputation for integrity by urging the government to reopen the investigation into a bribes-for-loans scandal involving Hanbo Steel Co, which collapsed under billions of dollars of debt in January.
Opposition parties have called the probe by state prosecutors a whitewash and are particularly incensed that it exonerated Kim's second son, Kim Hyun-chul.
The main opposition National Congress for New Politics has accused Hyun-chul of heavy involvement in state affairs as well as the Hanbo scandal.
The scandal has landed three of Kim's closest associates behind bars on bribery charges and further tarnished his image as a graft-buster.
The senior government official, who asked not to be identified, said Lee faced the task of pulling off a political coup to find a solution to the current crisis.
"Although Lee has a great chance to achieve his presidential ambitions, he will also have to go through a very serious test," he said.
There was a fresh twist on Tuesday in the race for the presidency when another of the "nine dragons" apparently suffered a stroke and was admitted to hospital.
Choi Hyung-woo, 61, a six-term member of parliament, headed a faction of Kim loyalists within the ruling party.

"Now Kim realises that his loyalists are unable to handle the crisis," an Asian diplomat said. "But Kim could always dump Lee later if he fails to deliver a solution. Kim will say: 'I have given you a chance and you blew it,'" he added.

Last month, Kim dumped four top presidential Blue House aides as part of a sweeping administration reshuffle designed to restore his credibility after the Hanbo scandal. He also changed his prime minister and reshuffled his cabinet.
